entry: Indigenous cacique and rebel leader in [[Peru]]. Of noble birth and a descendant of [[Túpac Amaru]], the last Inca of Vilcabamba, he was educated in [[Cusco]] and inherited the chieftainship of Surimana, Pampamarca, and Tungasuca after his father's death. He amassed a fortune through muleteering and petitioned colonial authorities to relieve the burdens of tribute and the mining mita, but his requests were ignored. After executing the corregidor Antonio de Arriaga for repeated abuses on November 4, 1780, he began a rebellion that spread through the Viceroyalty of Peru, extending into Upper Peru. The movement sought to end oppressive colonial practices rather than to win independence. On November 16, 1780, he decreed the abolition of slavery for Black people, the first such decree in Spanish America. He was executed after the rebellion ended in 1781. Later governments, especially during the regime of Juan Velasco Alvarado (1968–1975), made him a symbol of social justice.

Indigenous people of the [[Caribbean]], inhabiting most of the West Indies at the time of European contact. Part of the Arawak group of peoples, they lived in agricultural societies ruled by caciques, with matrilineal kinship and a religion centered on zemis. The name Taíno was first explicitly used in this sense by Constantine Samuel Rafinesque in 1836. Historians long asserted that the Taíno had disappeared or merged into African and Hispanic cultures, but attitudes began to change around the 21st century. Many people today identify as Taíno, most prominently in [[Puerto Rico]], [[Cuba]], and the [[Dominican Republic]].

Indian [[Sitcom|sitcom]] television series based on the weekly column *Duniya Ne Undha Chasma* by Tarak Mehta, published in the magazine *Chitralekha*. Produced by Asit Kumarr Modi, it premiered on July 28, 2008, on Sony SAB and is one of the longest-running television series in India. Set in Mumbai, it follows residents of the Gokuldham Co-operative Housing Society, a diverse community whose storylines center on everyday problems and festivals. A recurring theme follows Jethalal Champaklal Gada, whose comical troubles bring brief moments of relief before new challenges arise.

Family of true flies in the [[Insect|insect]] order Diptera, including horse flies and deer flies. Adults are often large and agile in flight, and the family occurs all over the world except for some islands and the polar regions. Females require a high [[Protein|protein]] diet and bite land vertebrates, including humans, to obtain the blood that enables them to produce eggs. Their mouthparts form a stout stabbing organ with two pairs of sharp cutting blades. Females can transfer blood-borne diseases, including anthrax among cattle and sheep, and can reduce growth rates in cattle if suitable shelters are not provided. The larvae are predaceous and grow in semiaquatic habitats. The insects appear in literature: [[Aeschylus]] depicts a gadfly driving Io to madness in *Prometheus Bound*, and [[Socrates]] later adopted the gadfly as an ironic mascot for his persistent questioning.

Domestic [[Cat|cat]] (*Felis catus*) with a coat pattern rather than a breed, marked by an M-shaped forehead marking and stripes by the eyes, cheeks, back, and legs. Four distinct patterns are known: mackerel, classic (or blotched), ticked, and spotted, each with a specific genetic basis. The patterns are connected to the coats of the African, European, and Asiatic wildcats, close relatives of the domestic cat. The English term originally referred to striped silk taffeta, derived through French and Arabic from the Attabiya district of [[Baghdad]], which was noted for its striped cloth.

King of Burma (r. 1530–1550) and founder of the [[Toungoo dynasty|First Toungoo Empire]]. From 1534 he and his deputy [[Bayinnaung]] conquered the Hanthawaddy kingdom by 1541, then extended his rule to the ancient capital of Pagan (Bagan) in 1544. His campaigns created the largest kingdom in Burma since the fall of the Pagan Empire in 1287, but his attempts to expand into Arakan (1545–1547) and Siam (1547–1549) fell short. He courted the Mons of Lower Burma, many of whom were appointed to the highest positions, and moved the capital to Pegu (Bago). He was assassinated on his 34th birthday on the orders of a close adviser, Smim Sawhtut, and the kingdom fell apart soon after. His successor and brother-in-law Bayinnaung restored it within two years and reunified the country.

Piece of furniture with a raised flat top, most commonly supported by one to four legs. Used for working, eating, or placing things, tables include dining tables, coffee tables, bedside tables, and drafting tables. Heights most commonly range from 18–30 inches (46–76 cm), often matching the height of [[Chair|chairs]] or bar stools. Folding tables collapse into a smaller volume, and drop-leaf sections can expand the surface of many dining tables. The word derives from Old English *tabele*, from Latin *tabula*. Some of the earliest tables were made by [[Ancient Egypt|Ancient Egyptians]] around 2500 BC from wood and alabaster. Greek and Roman tables were made of marble or wood and of metal, typically bronze or silver alloys. In medieval western Europe tables were often portable and set on trestles that were cleared away after meals. [[Charlemagne]] possessed three tables of silver and one of gold.

Racket sport played on a stationary table, also called ping-pong. Derived from [[Tennis|tennis]], it is played individually or in teams of two, with players alternately returning a light, hollow ball over a net with small rackets. Its emphasis on spin distinguishes it from other ball sports, and its small playing area allows play indoors in all climates. Table tennis has been an Olympic sport since 1988, and the International Table Tennis Federation (ITTF), founded in 1926, includes 226 member associations. The sport originated in Victorian England as an after-dinner parlor game. The name [[Onomatopoeia|ping-pong]] was in wide use before the British manufacturer J. Jaques & Son trademarked it in 1901. In the United States, Parker Brothers enforced its trademark in the 1920s, and associations changed their names to table tennis.

Large [[Spoon|spoon]] used for serving, and a cooking measure of volume. The international metric tablespoon, used in the UK and U.S., is exactly 15 mL. An Australian metric tablespoon is 20 mL, and the U.S. customary tablespoon is 1/2 U.S. fluid ounce, or approximately 14.8 mL. In most places one tablespoon equals three teaspoons, but in Australia it equals four. From about 1700 the place setting introduced the table-spoon, which was reserved for eating [[Soup|soup]]. In the late 19th century, in the UK, the word took on a second meaning as a much larger serving spoon.

Dishes and utensils used for setting a table, serving food, and dining. The term includes [[Cutlery|cutlery]], glassware, serving dishes, serving utensils, and decorative items. Their quality, variety, and number vary by culture, religion, cuisine, and occasion; some Middle Eastern, Indian, and Polynesian food cultures use bread or leaves as individual plates, sometimes without cutlery. In the United States, cutlery is usually called silverware or flatware. Ceramics such as earthenware, stoneware, bone china, and [[Porcelain|porcelain]] are common because glazes make them impermeable and easier to wash. Other materials include wood, metals such as pewter, tempered glass, and plastics. Cutlery is normally made of metal, especially stainless steel, and [[Chopsticks|chopsticks]] are made of wood, bamboo, metal, ivory, or plastic.

Ban or avoidance of an utterance or behavior by a social group, based on the group's sense that it is repulsive, offensive, sacred, or allowed only for certain people. Such prohibitions are present in virtually all societies, either explicitly in law or religion or implicitly in [[Social norm|social norms]]. Taboos are often meant to protect the individual, and many have ecological, medical, or religious origins. They can help use a resource efficiently, but when applied to only part of a community they can suppress that part. A taboo also fosters group cohesion and identity. The English term comes from the Polynesian *tapu*, meaning forbidden. English use dates to 1777, when the British explorer [[James Cook]] visited [[Tonga]]. [[Sigmund Freud]] speculated that [[Incest|incest]] and patricide were the only two universal taboos. Common taboos concern killing, sex, reproduction, the dead, and food, including [[Vegetarianism|vegetarianism]] and [[Kashrut|kashrut]].

City in East Azerbaijan province, northwestern [[Iran|Iran]] (pop., 2016: over 1.7 million). Capital of the province, the county, and the district, it is the sixth-most-populous city in Iran. It lies in the Quru River valley at 1,350 to 1,600 m (4,430 to 5,250 ft) above sea level and is the largest economic hub in northwest Iran. Its major industries include automobiles, machine tools, petrochemicals, textiles, and cement, and its handicrafts include hand-woven [[Carpet|carpets]] and jewelry. Most of its preserved historical sites belong to the Ilkhanid, Safavid, and Qajar periods, and its Bazaar is a [[World Heritage Site]]. From the early modern era, Tabriz was pivotal in the development of the [[Caucasus]], [[Anatolia|Eastern Anatolia]], and Central Iran. The Qajar dynasty ceded Caucasian territories to Imperial [[Russia|Russia]] after two Russo-Persian Wars in the first half of the 19th century.

Indian actress known for complex, often troubled women in Hindi films. Widely regarded as one of Hindi cinema's most accomplished actresses, she has received two National Film Awards, seven Filmfare Awards (including a record five Critics Awards for Best Actress), and two Filmfare Awards South. She was awarded the Padma Shri, India's fourth-highest civilian award, in 2011. She won the National Film Award for Best Actress for *Maachis* (1996) and a second for *Chandni Bar* (2001). Her biggest commercial successes include *Andhadhun* (2018) and *Drishyam 2* (2022).

Heart rate that exceeds the normal resting rate, also called tachyarrhythmia. In adults a resting heart rate over 100 beats per minute is generally accepted as tachycardia. Higher rates may be normal, as with [[Exercise|exercise]], or abnormal, as with electrical problems in the heart. A rapid rate lets the heart pump less efficiently and raises its oxygen demand, and tachycardia can lead to fainting. An [[Electrocardiography|electrocardiogram]] classifies it as narrow complex, such as [[Atrial fibrillation|atrial fibrillation]], or wide complex, such as ventricular tachycardia.

Hypothetical particle that always travels faster than light. Physicists posit that such particles cannot exist because they are inconsistent with the known laws of physics. If they did, they could send signals into the past, violating [[Causality (physics)|causality]] and leading to paradoxes such as the grandfather paradox. Tachyons would increase in speed as their energy decreased and would require infinite energy to slow to the [[Speed of light|speed of light]]. No verifiable experimental evidence supports them. The term was coined in 1967 by Gerald Feinberg for excitations of a quantum field with imaginary mass, which do not in fact propagate faster than light.

Roman historian and politician, regarded by modern scholars as one of the greatest Roman historians. His two major works, the *Annals* and the *Histories*, originally formed a continuous narrative of the [[Roman Empire]] from the death of [[Augustus]] (14 AD) to the end of [[Domitian]]'s reign (96 AD). The surviving portions of the *Annals* focus on the reigns of [[Tiberius]], [[Claudius]], and [[Nero]], and on the Year of the Four Emperors (69 AD). His other works include *Agricola*, a biography of his father-in-law, the general responsible for much of the Roman conquest of Britain, and *Germania*, on the origins and location of the Germans.

Traditional Mexican dish of a small, hand-sized tortilla folded around a filling and eaten by hand. Corn- or wheat-based tortillas hold fillings of beef, pork, chicken, seafood, beans, vegetables, or cheese, garnished with salsa, guacamole, sour cream, [[Coriander|coriander]], onion, or chiles. Tacos are a common form of antojitos, or Mexican street food, that have spread around the world. They differ from burritos, which are larger and rolled, and from tostadas, whose tortillas are fried before filling. The origins of the taco are debated. Some argue that indigenous people of the Valley of [[Mexico|Mexico]] ate tacos filled with small fish before the Spanish arrived, while others trace the dish to 18th-century [[Silver|silver]] miners. [[Hernán Cortés]] arranged a taco feast for his captains in Coyoacán, which Bernal Díaz del Castillo documented.

Port city in [[Washington (state)|Washington]], United States (pop., 2020: 219,346). County seat of Pierce County, it lies on Puget Sound about 30 miles (48 km) from [[Seattle]]. Its Port of Tacoma is Washington's largest port and a center of [[International trade|international trade]]. The name derives from the nearby [[Mount Rainier]]. Chosen in 1873 as the western terminus of the Northern Pacific Railroad, the city adopted the motto "When rails meet sails." The Tacoma Narrows Bridge collapsed in 1940, earning the nickname "Galloping Gertie." Downtown has been revitalized since the 1990s.

Larval stage in the life cycle of an [[Amphibian|amphibian]]. Most tadpoles are fully aquatic, though some amphibians have terrestrial tadpoles. Tadpoles have fish-like features absent in adult amphibians, such as a lateral line, [[Gill|gills]], and swimming tails. During [[Metamorphosis|metamorphosis]] they develop functional [[Lung|lungs]] for breathing air, and their diet changes drastically. Some frogs undergo direct development, emerging from eggs as fully formed froglets, while others hatch as tadpoles under the mother's skin or are kept in a pouch until after metamorphosis. Frog tadpoles are usually herbivorous, while those of [[Salamander|salamanders]] and [[Caecilian|caecilians]] are carnivorous. Although tadpoles have no hard skeletons, fossil tadpoles have been found dating back to the Middle Jurassic. The name comes from Middle English *taddepol*, meaning "toad head."

Founder of the [[Goryeo]] dynasty of [[Korea]], who ruled from 918 to 943. Born Wang Kŏn in Songak (modern Kaesong), he came from a powerful maritime merchant family of Goguryeo descent. Modern historians consider his ancestors Goguryeo lords who conducted trade with China for generations. He began his career under Kung Ye, leading campaigns against Later Baekje, including a naval campaign at Keumsung in 903. In 913 he was appointed prime minister of Taebong, the kingdom Kung Ye had helped found. He unified the Later Three Kingdoms in 936, when the king of Later Baekje surrendered. His Ten Mandates to his heirs prioritized national unity over familial vendettas and relations with neighboring powers such as the Khitan Liao dynasty.

First monarch of [[Joseon]], who reigned from 1392 to 1398. A military general under the declining [[Goryeo]] dynasty, he repelled Japanese pirates and Red Turban invaders and pushed Mongol remnants off the peninsula. He overthrew the Goryeo regime and ascended to the throne in 1392. His reign emphasized continuity over change: no new institutions were created and no massive purges occurred, and the new dynasty was largely dominated by the same families that had served Goryeo. He re-established amicable ties with Japan and improved relations with [[Ming dynasty|Ming China]]. He abdicated six years after taking the throne, amid strife between his sons. After the Korean Empire was established, he was honored as Emperor Ko.

Korean [[Martial arts|martial art]] and combat sport centered on kicking and punching. Its name combines *tae* ("strike with foot"), *kwon* ("strike with hand"), and *do* ("the art or way"). Patterns, called hyeong, poomsae, or teul, demonstrate kicks, punches, and blocks, while kyorugi is the full-contact sparring seen in the Olympics. It is primarily unarmed, and practitioners wear a uniform known as a dobok. It was developed in the 1940s and 1950s by Korean martial artists with experience in [[Karate|karate]] and [[Chinese martial arts]]. The Korea Taekwondo Association, formed in 1959 by representatives of nine original kwans, is the oldest governing body. The International Taekwon-Do Federation (ITF), founded by Choi Hong-hi in 1966, and World Taekwondo, which governs the sport at the Olympic level, are the main international bodies. Kyorugi has been an Olympic event since 2000.

Playground game in which one or more players chase others to tag and mark them out of play, typically by touching them with a hand. The tagged player becomes "it" and continues the chase. Most forms have no teams, scores, or equipment, and variations include freeze tag, chain tag, and rules that prevent tag-backs. Tag-like games have been played since at least the fourth century BC; the Greek poet Erinna described a game in which a child called the "tortoise" chases others. In India, kho-kho has been played since at least the fourth century BC, and aspects of [[Kabaddi|kabaddi]] and kho-kho are believed to appear in the [[Mahabharata]]. The game is called "tig" in [[Yorkshire]] and [[Scotland]], and "tag" in the United States. Major modern competitions include World Chase Tag, the Pro Kabaddi League, and Ultimate Kho Kho.

Austronesian language spoken in the [[Philippines|Philippines]]. It is a first language of the ethnic Tagalog people, who make up about a quarter of the population, and a second language for most of the rest. Its standardized form, Filipino, is the national language and one of the country's two official languages, alongside English. Tagalog is a Central Philippine language, closely related to the Bikol and Visayan languages and more distantly to Malay and Hawaiian. It follows the trigger system of morphosyntactic alignment common among Philippine languages and has nine basic parts of speech. The first complete book in Tagalog, the *Doctrina Christiana*, was printed in 1593 in both Baybayin script and a Latin transcription. During the 333 years of Spanish rule, clergymen wrote grammars and dictionaries of the language.

Genus of about 50 species of annual or perennial, mostly herbaceous plants in the family [[Asteraceae|Asteraceae]], many known as marigolds. Native to Central and Southern [[Mexico|Mexico]] and several other [[Latin America|Latin American]] countries, they were originally called *cempōhualxōchitl* by the Nahua people. [[Carl Linnaeus|Carl Linnaeus]] formally named the genus in 1753. Most species have pinnate green leaves and blooms in golden, orange, yellow, and white colors. The florets of *Tagetes erecta* are rich in the [[Carotenoid|carotenoid]] lutein and are used as a food color in the European Union. *T. minuta*, originally from South America, is used for an essential oil for the perfume industry and is considered a noxious invasive species in some areas.
